newsitem.title: USA: Republicans hit Clinton budget, say won't balance.
newsitem.headline: Republicans hit Clinton budget, say won't balance.

text.p: Republican congressional leaders on Thursday gave a negative, sceptical reception to President Bill Clinton's new federal budget and said would not eliminate the federal deficit by 2002 as Clinton says.

"It does not balance in the year 2002," said Representative John Kasich, an Ohio Republican who chairs the influential House of Representatives Budget Committee. He added that Clinton's budget was not the bold formula for change the majority Republicans in Congress had hoped for.

Kasich said he and other Republicans had had high hopes Clinton would provide a bold plan for ending the "era of big government" and providing real tax cuts and deficit reduction, but concluded: "We just really do not have the kind of bold document that we would like to see that would be a message to people that there really is change in Washington."

At a news conference providing an initial Republican leadership response to Clinton's proposal, he and Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici of New Mexico both said the proposal was not entirely bad. "I do not think this budget is dead on arrival," said Domenici, who predicted compromises would be worked out and agreement reached.

But their emphasis was highly critical. "I thought we were really going to have a very bold budget and I dont think it is," Domenici said. "... "We are going to have to do a lot of working together to bridge the gap that is clear between that (Clinton) budget and what we feel will be good for the future of our country."

Although Clinton maintains his new budget plan would eliminate federal deficits by the second year of the new millennium -- and keep it in balance for years -- Kasich said: "When the Congressional Budget Office takes a look at this it is my expectation that they will say in fact the president's budget is not balanced using the same starting point as we will use." Domenici went further, saying he expected the CBO would find Clinton's budget $50 billion in deficit in 2002.
